intro: Stage conventions carry meaning across the room before a performer speaks.
alt: Three stages feature a spare pine backdrop, a red theatrical setting and rich red-and-jade performance dress.

variants.name: Noh
variants.look: A spare cypress setting and economical gesture concentrate attention on the performer.
variants.history: Noh developed into a major Japanese theater form in the medieval period, combining chant, music and highly codified movement.
variants.when: Look for how a small shift in angle or pace changes a performance.
variants.why: With few competing details, spectators can attend to subtle gesture and sound.

variants.name: Kabuki
variants.look: A forceful held pose and vivid stage makeup project across the stage.
variants.history: Kabuki developed in the Edo period and uses striking makeup, staging and movement. A held mie accentuates a dramatic moment.
variants.when: Use a sharply defined posture to hold the audience’s attention at a turning point.
variants.why: A fixed posture punctuates the flow of performance and makes a dramatic peak readable.

variants.name: Chinese opera
variants.look: Costume shapes and articulated hand poses make the gesture visible.
variants.history: Chinese opera spans many regional traditions. Peking opera, one influential form, combines vocal, musical and athletic skills with intricate codes of costume and makeup.
variants.when: Look for how costume, gesture and role convey action within limited staging.
variants.why: Repeatedly learned visual cues let audiences recognize a role and follow its actions from afar.
variants.period: Many centuries of regional forms; Peking opera developed in the Qing period
